title: The CDC and the Measles Mystery: Why Some Doctors Are Worried
summary:
Imagine you're playing a game, and the scorekeeper suddenly changes the score — but won't tell you why. That's kind of how some doctors feel about the CDC right now.

The CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) is the U.S. government's main health agency. It's supposed to tell everyone — doctors, schools, and families — the truth about diseases.

Right now, measles is spreading in the U.S. more than it has in decades. That's a big deal because measles is a very contagious virus. It can make kids really sick.

Recently, two people died from measles in Pennsylvania. State health officials said measles caused the deaths. But then Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who leads the Department of Health and Human Services, questioned whether measles really caused them. And the CDC removed the deaths from its website.

That's unusual. Normally, the CDC trusts the state's decision and shares the information to warn people.

Dr. Demetre Daskalakis used to work at the CDC. He quit last year because he said politics was getting in the way of science. Now he says, "Red flag. Red alert." He thinks it's dangerous.

Other experts worry too. Dr. Anne Zink says states and the federal government aren't working together like they should. If people can't trust the CDC's numbers, they might not know how to stay safe.

The CDC has a new director, Dr. Erica Schwartz. Some doctors hope she'll speak up about vaccines. The CDC didn't answer NPR's questions.
why_it_matters: Knowing who to trust for health information helps your family and your school know when to get shots — and shows how confusing things get when politics mixes with science.

background_read: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known — one sick person can infect many people in the same room, and it can cause serious problems like pneumonia.
The CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — the U.S. government's main public health agency, based in Atlanta) tracks diseases and gives advice that doctors, schools, and families follow.

Robert F. Kennedy Jr. leads the Department of Health and Human Services (the part of the U.S. government in charge of health programs) and has raised questions about vaccines, which many doctors disagree with.
Article_Structure: WHO: The CDC, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. (who leads the Department of Health and Human Services), Pennsylvania state health officials, and worried doctors like Dr. Demetre Daskalakis and Dr. Anne Zink.
WHAT: Measles is spreading more than it has in decades, and after two deaths in Pennsylvania the CDC removed them from its website instead of sharing the warning with everyone.
WHERE: Pennsylvania and across the United States.
WHY: If people can't trust the CDC's numbers, they may not know how to stay safe from a very contagious virus.
